source.title: Scaling Law for Recommendation Models: Towards General-purpose User Representations
source.authors: Kyuyong Shin; Hanock Kwak; S. Kim; M. Ramström; Jisu Jeong; Jung-Woo Ha; Kyung-Min Kim

record.file_problem: No major problem; the text includes flattened tables and figures, but the study is readable and complete.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures scaling in recommendation user representations, a setting beyond language-model text pretraining, and reports its own results.
record.gate_note: The study reports a pretraining test-loss curve against compute and a relationship between pretraining and downstream losses. It also reports online PCR outcomes for two CLUE sizes. Benchmark leaderboard and architecture-ablation results are not recorded as scaling results. The figure-only scaling plots do not provide extractable numeric coordinates or fitted exponents.
record.test_reason: The study trains contrastive user-behaviour encoders across compute scales. It reports pretraining test loss against PF-days, which it calls a power law. It also relates downstream out-of-distribution loss to pretraining loss and reports downstream and online results across model and data scale. This is a new setting, recommendation user representations, with its own results on the power-law form (V5) and on downstream predictability (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that performance does not depend on model size alone, that batch size and sequence length matter considerably, and that all four factors must scale up in tandem. They read the online 120M > 15M result as the scaling law holding online.
record.recipe_differences: Uses contrastive learning for user representations from behavior logs and measures pretraining test loss against PF-days; it does not use autoregressive language-model pretraining or language-model cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: The study varies model size, batch size, sequence length and training-data size, and reports that these factors influence performance; it also reports an effect from batch shuffling. It does not report sensitivity of fitted exponents to fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: In contrastive user-representation learning, batch size (the number of negatives) acts as a bottleneck. Scaling is more complex than model size alone, and batch shuffling has considerable effects.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In contrastive pretraining, batch size is a scaling factor that can bottleneck loss and downstream gains independently of parameters and data.

record.problems: The scaling plots provide no extractable numeric coordinates or fitted exponents, and the text reports no uncertainty estimates for these results. The experiment concerns recommendation user representations rather than language models.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 report downstream benchmark comparisons but do not compare model scale. Table 5 reports an encoder-architecture comparison using downstream metrics rather than the loss named in the claim. Other resource-allocation plots are not included as separate rows because their plotted values are not numerically stated.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss is not studied.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger runs.
No compute-optimal parameter/token allocation or exponents are reported. The authors only say all factors should scale in tandem.
There is no depth/width-at-fixed-parameters loss comparison. Table 5 compares single vs stacked encoders using downstream metrics.
Image/video, repeated data and fine-tuning regimes are not tested. No exponent is fitted, and no separate parameter- or data-only loss laws are reported.
No fitting-method or parameter-counting comparisons are made.

missing.what: ICLT MRR vs model size (4M–160M) at fixed sequence length and batch size, and vs batch size and sequence length. The authors say model size alone does not dominate performance.
ICLT MRR vs computation for different batch sizes and sequence lengths across model sizes
ICLT performance vs training-data fraction (1%–100%) with and without shuffling. More data strictly improves downstream performance.

record.verdict_notes: The domain is recommendation, not language models, and the objective is contrastive (CLIP-style). All scaling evidence is figure-only, with no fitted exponents or uncertainty. The 15M/120M online comparison has two points and a five-day test, so it is weak evidence for predictability.

versions.untested_parts: The study is not about language-model held-out pretraining loss and does not test loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute with the other factors non-bottlenecking.
No small-run fitted law is used to predict the loss of much larger runs.
The study varies resource factors but does not identify a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute or fit growth exponents for that allocation.
The architecture comparison reports downstream recommendation metrics, not held-out pretraining loss at a fixed parameter count across depth and width variations.
Tests a contrastive user-representation setting using user behavior data; it does not test image/video models, repeated data, or fine-tuning and transfer regimes as scaling-law settings.
Tests downstream recommendation losses and online PCR engagement, not predictability across other downstream task families or language-model benchmarks.
The study varies training factors but does not compare fitting methods or parameter-count conventions, report fitted exponents, or show that curves bend away from a fitted power law.

rows.subject: CLUE
rows.operation_detail: Varied total training computation and measured pretraining-distribution test loss.
rows.measure: Pretraining test loss as a function of computation
rows.value: Figure only; the text describes a power-law decrease in pretraining test loss with computation when not bottlenecked by other factors.
rows.note: The figure plots test loss against PF-days, but no numerical coordinates or fitted exponent are stated.
rows.check: Figure only, with no fitted exponent or coordinates. The compute axis spans about 1e-5 to 1e-1 PF-days. Compute is varied jointly through model size, batch size and sequence length, and the power law is claimed only 'when not bottlenecked by other factors'.

relationships.condition: Contrastive user-representation pretraining on behaviour logs, loss vs compute (PF-days), when not bottlenecked
relationships.reason: Pretraining test loss falls with compute over about four orders of magnitude; the authors call it power-law (r1). The evidence is figure only, with no exponent.
relationships.display_finding: Pretraining test loss decreased with compute over approximately four orders of magnitude in a trend the authors described as power-law.

relationships.condition: Transfer to downstream data with a different distribution
relationships.reason: Lower pretraining loss is associated with lower out-of-distribution loss in a strong trend (r2). The downstream loss range is narrow.
relationships.display_finding: Lower pretraining loss was strongly associated with lower out-of-distribution loss over a narrow downstream loss range.

relationships.condition: Online PCR CTR, New/Cold/Total segments, 15M vs 120M
relationships.reason: 120M beats 15M (4.5 vs 4.1, 13.4 vs 11.0, 7.3 vs 6.5) (r3–r6, r9, r10). There are only two sizes and no uncertainty is reported.
relationships.display_finding: The larger model improved New, Cold and Total segment metrics from 4.1 to 4.5, 11.0 to 13.4, and 6.5 to 7.3, respectively, without reported uncertainty.

relationships.reason: The gain from 8x more parameters is negligible (10.5% vs 10.7%) (r7, r8).
relationships.display_finding: An eightfold parameter increase changes the reported CTR result only from 10.5% to 10.7%.

relationships.condition: ICLT downstream MRR as model size varies (Figure 2a)
relationships.reason: From the text, not rows: downstream performance 'does not depend dominantly on model capacity alone'. Batch size and sequence length also matter.
relationships.display_finding: Downstream MRR depends on batch size and sequence length as well as model capacity.
